title: Maternal Sepsis in Pregnancy or Postpartum

pathophysiology.summary: Maternal sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction from infection during pregnancy, childbirth, the post-abortion period or the postpartum period. A dysregulated host response causes vasodilatation, capillary leak, myocardial depression and microvascular thrombosis; normal pregnancy physiology masks early signs.
keyMechanisms: Pregnancy raises heart rate and lowers BP and WBC thresholds overlap with normal values — most women who died of sepsis were afebrile and had delayed escalation (SMFM).

Common sources: antepartum — pyelonephritis, pneumonia, chorioamnionitis; postpartum — endometritis, wound infection, mastitis, urinary tract infection. Necrotising soft-tissue infection and group A Streptococcus cause rapid toxin-mediated shock.
Lactate rises with tissue hypoperfusion; uterine infection may need delivery/evacuation for source control.
Sepsis increases thrombotic risk (pregnancy is already prothrombotic) — give pharmacological VTE prophylaxis in septic shock.
Fetal compromise usually reflects maternal hypoperfusion — resuscitating the mother is the best fetal treatment.

symptoms: Fever or hypothermia (may be absent), rigors, feeling unwell.
Abdominal or pelvic pain, offensive lochia or vaginal discharge, wound pain/redness.
Cough, breathlessness; dysuria, loin pain; breast pain.
Diarrhoea and vomiting (early sign of toxin-mediated GAS infection).
physicalSigns: Tachycardia above 100, tachypnoea, hypotension (SBP below 90), altered mental state.
Uterine tenderness, wound cellulitis, fetal tachycardia.
redFlags: SBP below 90 mmHg or MAP below 65 despite fluids (septic shock)
Lactate above 4 mmol/L (MOH) — any raised lactate needs action
Altered mental status; SpO2 falling; oliguria
Rapidly spreading skin changes, severe pain or toxic shock features (group A Streptococcus)
Signs of intra-amniotic infection — delivery needed regardless of gestation
precipitants: Caesarean birth, prolonged rupture of membranes, retained products, invasive procedures.
Group A Streptococcus contact (sore throat in family).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Hypertension, raised liver enzymes, low platelets — can mimic organ dysfunction.
Hypotension from bleeding; check blood loss and Hb.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: At recognition; repeat to guide resuscitation
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Recommended in all suspected maternal sepsis (SMFM 1B).

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and escalate
actions: Consider sepsis with any unexplained organ dysfunction and suspected infection — even without fever.
Treat as an emergency: senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, critical care; HDU/ICU for septic shock (MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: First hour
actions: Oxygen to maintain saturation; left lateral tilt if pregnant beyond 20 weeks.
Blood and source cultures, lactate — then broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 h.
Hypotension or hypoperfusion: 1–2 L balanced crystalloid within the first 3 h (SMFM); reassess with dynamic measures (avoid overload — pulmonary oedema risk in pregnancy). No starches or gelatin.

clinicalManagement.title: Empiric antibiotics by likely source (SMFM Table 4)
actions: Unknown source or septic shock: piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 h (or a carbapenem) ± vancomycin if MRSA risk.
Chorioamnionitis: ampicillin + gentamicin; add clindamycin or metronidazole if caesarean birth.
Endometritis: ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole (or clindamycin); alternatively ceftriaxone/cefotaxime + metronidazole.
Pyelonephritis: gentamicin + ampicillin, or carbapenem / piperacillin–tazobactam monotherapy.
Necrotising soft-tissue infection: vancomycin + piperacillin–tazobactam; if group A Streptococcus or Clostridium: penicillin G + clindamycin.
Narrow to cultures; shorter courses are usually adequate once source controlled.

clinicalManagement.title: Septic shock
actions: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in pregnancy and postpartum; target MAP 65 mmHg.
Persistent vasopressor need: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV (50 mg every 6 h or infusion).
Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (LMWH) in septic shock.
Insulin if glucose above 180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L).

clinicalManagement.title: Source control and delivery
actions: Rapidly identify/exclude an anatomical source; drain abscesses, debride necrotising infection.
Uterine source (intra-amniotic infection, retained products): prompt delivery or evacuation regardless of gestation.
Sepsis alone is not an indication for immediate delivery — decide on gestation and maternal/fetal condition; stabilise the mother first. Give antenatal steroids if preterm birth is likely.

learningObjectives: Recognise maternal sepsis early, start the first-hour bundle and achieve source control.
pitfalls: Delaying antibiotics for cultures or imaging.
Missing group A Streptococcus (diarrhoea, severe pain).
Rushing delivery in an unstable mother when the source is not uterine.
keyPoints: Think sepsis without fever — unexplained organ dysfunction + infection.
Find and control the source — uterine source means delivery/evacuation.
